## Sonntag, 20:15 Uhr

Since **29 November 1970**, Germany has settled in on Sunday nights for *Tatort* ("crime scene"), the longest-running crime drama on German-language TV.

- **1,311 episodes**, ten regional broadcasters, dozens of detective teams
- An episode list handled by many people over 55 years

Today the list itself is the crime scene. **You have 45 minutes.**

::: notes
**0:00–2:00 · Welcome + hook**

- While people sit down, the link to the evidence file should already be on screen or in the chat (see the Facilitator Guide). Ask everyone to sign in to office.com now.
- Quick show of hands: anyone watched Tatort? Real, big, multilingual data assembled by many hands over 55 years. That's exactly how messy data happens.
- Fun fact from the dataset: episode 25, *Tote Taube in der Beethovenstraße* (1973), was directed by Samuel Fuller and ran in US cinemas.
- Hand out the Evidence Card now, one per person.
:::

## How Today Works

::: {.agenda}
| | | |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-flight | Open your copy of the evidence | 5 min |
| Sprint 1 | Survey the scene | 5 min |
| Sprint 2 | Clear the scene | 7 min |
| Sprint 3 | Hidden characters | 7 min |
| Sprint 4 | Unmask the aliases | 7 min |
| Sprint 5 | Time of the crime | 7 min |
| Debrief | What's left, and how to finish | 3 min |
:::

Each sprint: **1-minute briefing → you work, timer on screen → checkpoint**. Fell behind? Every sprint has a **catch-up sheet** so you can jump straight back in.

::: notes
**2:00–3:00 · How today works**

- This is the contract with the room. Short briefings, then they work on their own while the timer runs. When the timer hits zero, we all compare numbers and move on together, wherever you are.
- Stress the catch-up sheets: nobody is left behind for more than one sprint. Falling behind is normal, not failure.
- Some of the case is left for later. The "On Your Own" guide documents every remaining step.
:::

- The grey tabs at the end are the catch-up sheets. Don't open them yet: they're spoilers for the next sprint.

- This is where in-person workshops lose 10 minutes. Have the link on screen as a QR code and a short URL, and in the room chat if there is one.

- If the copy option is missing for someone, fallback: File → Download, then upload to their own OneDrive (office.com → Upload).
- Duplicate tab = chain of custody. In the browser there's no "close without saving".
- Walk the room. When most hands are up, move on. Anyone still stuck: pair them with a neighbour for now and come back to them.
:::

## [Sprint 1]{.tag} Look Before You Touch

- Scroll to the **bottom** and the **far right**. Where does the data really end?
- **Data → Filter**, then open each column's drop-down. Every odd spelling is listed there.
- Click a cell and compare the **formula bar** with what the cell shows.
- Left-aligned "numbers" and "dates" are usually **text**.

::: {.clue}
Write the clue down before you fix anything. Detectives who fix as they look lose track of what they found.
:::

::: notes
**9:00–10:00 · Briefing (1 min)**

- [DEMO, 30 s] Data → Filter, open the `Sender` drop-down: `wdr`, `W.D.R.`, `Westdeutscher Rundfunk`… That's the moment that sells filters.
- Don't fix anything in this sprint. Just look.
:::

Call out your clues. Did anyone find…

:::: {.incremental}
- three title rows above the header and junk columns on the right?
- the **same episode twice**?

- dates that are left-aligned **text** in two different formats, and numbers like `25901`?
- titles in ALL CAPS, `n/a`, `unbekannt` and `NULL` instead of blanks?
::::

Today we chase the first four. The rest are in the **On Your Own** guide.

::: notes
**13:00–14:00 · Checkpoint (1 min)**

- Take 3–4 clues from the room, then reveal the list one line at a time (each click shows the next).
- Name the plan: sprint 2 clears the scene, 3 hidden characters, 4 aliases, 5 dates. Everything else is documented for later.

## [Sprint 2]{.tag} Clear the Scene

- Row 1 **is** the header: delete the title rows above it
- Headers: short, unique, no stray spaces or ALL CAPS (match the `Data_Dictionary`)
- Delete columns you don't need
- **Insert → Table**: new formulas fill the whole column automatically
- **Data → Remove Duplicates**, all columns ticked = only *exact* copies go

::: {.warn}
Same title ≠ duplicate. *Die Abrechnung* is the title of three different episodes.
:::

::: notes
**14:00–15:30 · Briefing (1.5 min)**

- Why title rows matter: they break filters, tables and pivot tables.
- Why a Table: from Sprint 3 on, every formula fills down the whole column by itself. That's what makes this doable in 45 minutes.
- Remove Duplicates with all columns = only rows identical in every cell. Choosing fewer columns is a judgement call about what "the same record" means.
:::

- Common trap: deleting the junk columns *after* Remove Duplicates. `Import_ID` is different on every row, so Excel finds 0 duplicates. Order matters: clear the scene first.
- Headers matter now because the formulas in the next sprints use them by name (`[@Titel]`). A header with a stray space breaks the formula.
- Ignore the yellow highlights for now (On Your Own guide).
:::

## [Sprint 3]{.tag} Hidden Characters

**Helper columns:** never overwrite the evidence. Clean in a *new* column beside it, compare, keep both.

```
=TRIM(text)                       removes leading, trailing & double spaces
=TRIM(SUBSTITUTE(text, UNICHAR(160), " "))
                                  …and the invisible non-breaking space
=LEN(old)<>LEN(new)               TRUE if cleaning changed something
```

::: {.small .muted}
Character 160 looks exactly like a space and comes in when data is copied from the web. `TRIM` alone ignores it.
:::

::: notes
**21:00–22:30 · Briefing + the one demo that matters (1.5 min)**

- [DEMO] The copy routine from the Formulas sheet, once, slowly: click the green cell → click in the formula bar → Ctrl/⌘+A, Ctrl/⌘+C → Esc → type `Titel_Clean` in the first empty header cell to the right of the table → Enter → click the cell below → Ctrl/⌘+V → Enter. The whole column fills.
- If the column doesn't fill by itself: a small lightning icon offers "Overwrite all cells in this column". Or double-click the fill handle.
- We keep the helper columns rather than pasting values back. Fewer steps, and the original stays beside the clean version for comparison. The On Your Own guide shows how to swap them in at the end.
:::

## [Sprint 4]{.tag} Unmask the Aliases

`wdr`, `W.D.R.` and `Westdeutscher Rundfunk` are all **WDR**. Don't Find & Replace 55 times: use a **reference table**.

```
=XLOOKUP(what, where to look, what to bring back, "if not found")

=XLOOKUP(TRIM(TEXTBEFORE([@Sender], "/", , , , [@Sender])),
         Known_Aliases!A:A, Known_Aliases!B:B, "CHECK")
```

- `TEXTBEFORE(…, "/")`: co-productions like `SWR/SRF` → lead broadcaster `SWR`
- `"CHECK"`: anything not on the list is flagged, not guessed

::: notes
**28:00–29:30 · Briefing (1.5 min)**

- Read XLOOKUP aloud in plain English: "look up this broadcaster in column A of Known_Aliases and bring back its code from column B; if it isn't there, write CHECK."
- XLOOKUP ignores capitalisation, so `wdr` matches `WDR`. That's why the alias list doesn't need every case variant.
- The empty arguments (`, , , ,`) skip options we don't need. The last one says "if there's no slash, use the whole cell". They'll copy it, not type it.
- The reference-table idea is the most transferable skill of the night: majors, country names, department codes, survey answers…
:::

## [Sprint 5]{.tag} Time of the Crime

| What you see | What it is |
|---|---|
| `1970-11-29` right-aligned | a real date |
| `25901` | a real date shown as a number (*General* format) |
| `29.11.1970` left-aligned | text, German day.month.year |
| `1970-11-29` left-aligned | text, ISO year-month-day |

`DATE(year, month, day)` rebuilds text dates and **never guesses** your region. Then check: Tatort began **29 Nov 1970**. Earlier, or in the future? **Impossible.**

::: notes
**35:00–36:30 · Briefing (1.5 min)**

- Excel stores dates as numbers: days since 1900. So `25901` is 29 November 1970, the very first Tatort.
- DATEVALUE guesses using the computer's regional settings; DATE never guesses.
- The formula on the Formulas sheet uses LET: `d` is a nickname for the date cell so it doesn't have to be repeated. Read it aloud: already a date? keep it. Third character a dot? German. Otherwise ISO.
- Plausibility checks are the habit: you can't always know the right value, but you can know an impossible one. Don't guess a fix; flag it.
:::

:::

::: notes
**36:30–41:30 · Work (5 min)**

- A date showing as `#####` just means the column is too narrow: double-click the column border.
- One impossible date comes out as the year 3799: the typo `1899` plus Excel's rule that years below 1900 get 1900 added. A great "don't trust the output" moment if someone spots it.
- Don't fix the impossible dates. Flag them in the Case Log; the right date has to come from a source.
:::

- **A** · Yellow highlights
- **B** · Episode numbers & the last 6 duplicates
- **C** · Case numbers stored as text
- **D** · Writers: line breaks & `n/a`
- **E** · Directors & `NULL` notes
- **F** · ALL CAPS titles
- **G** · Investigators & guest stars

::: notes
**42:00–43:00 · What's left**

- Each lead takes 3–5 minutes with the guide; they can do it later today while it's fresh. The guide has the formulas and the expected numbers, so they can check themselves.
- Their copy stays in their OneDrive, so they can pick up exactly where they left off.
:::

## Good Habits

- **Secure the scene**: raw data is read-only
- **Look before you touch**, and write down what you see
- **Clean in helper columns**, compare, then swap in
- **Don't trust what Excel shows you**: trust `LEN`, filters and the formula bar
- **Don't guess**: flag what you can't verify
- **Document everything**: the Case Log is part of the evidence

::: notes
**43:00–44:00 · Wrap-up**

- These habits carry straight over to R, Python or anything else. Mention the R + AI workshop for anyone who wants to automate this.
:::
